place.zh: 沂中医 · 城里的医院 · 十一月底
place.en: Yizhong · the hospital in town · late November

setup.zh: 「凑数的。」他背着人「闭关三日」，晨脉八十八，回了一个「好」，蹲完了。夜里尿成可乐色：横纹肌溶解。出院那天，阿禾的纸上三条。
setup.en: "Just making up the numbers." He trains three days in secret; morning pulse 88; he answers "OK" and finishes the squats anyway. That night his urine is cola: rhabdomyolysis. On discharge, three lines on Ahe's paper.

recap.zh: 练太猛，横纹肌溶解，住院三天；「数是你自己报的」——晨脉七十以下，才许摸球。
recap.en: Overtrained, rhabdomyolysis, three days in hospital; "you report the numbers yourself" — under seventy in the morning, then the ball.

zh: 晨脉回到七十以下，才许摸球。
en: Under seventy in the morning — then the ball.

story.zh:
十一月二十一日，星期六，小组赛第三轮。替补席上摆着一排纸杯，杯口朝下，杯底写着号——阿禾的规矩：谁上过场，下来喝水，就把自己那只翻过来。沈芒拄着拐坐在看台上数了两遍：十一只。他那只「0」，没摆上去。

针推赢了，A 组头名——进了前四，明年还有针推这支队。记分台后头，阿禾把本子合上，两只手按在上头，按了好一会儿，才又打开。隔壁半场，中药学院也赢了，B 组头名。散场时，马小宝晃过来，拿摇杯点了点他的拐：「零号。一队报十二个人，少一个报不上名——你就是来凑数的。」古籍部那一夜，两个人谁也没提；马小宝待他倒比从前更随便了，像要把那一夜找补回来。

这话一个字也没说错，所以格外疼。针推那张报名表，是交名单那天夜里十一点四十，阿禾差一个人，才把他的身份证号填上去的。他攥着拐，指节攥得发白，脸上还得笑着；那个篮板，那个烧着的东西，叫这两个字一浇，滋地一声，灭了。

可疼完了，他心里竟悄悄松了一下：凑数的，没人看，不用站上罚球线，不用叫几百双眼睛一齐盯着。这一松，他自己也吓了一跳，赶紧按了回去，谁也没告诉。

那天夜里，老蔡的手机从上铺垂下来，屏幕停在一行字上：「少年闭关三日，出关连破两境。」

他盯着那行字看了很久。山洞他没有；三天，他有。

半决赛在二十八号。阿禾给他的功课只有一样：闭眼单脚站。这一礼拜，他从三秒站到了二十几秒，阿禾说站稳三十秒才算接上。可他要让她看见的，不能只是一只站得稳的脚——一只站得稳的脚，还是凑数的。他给自己也排了个「闭关三日」：晚上七点上二楼健身房，练到十点关门；脚踝不跳，别的全练。中秋办的那张卡还没过期；那个钟点健身房里只有几个考研的在跑步机上走路，没人认得他。还有一条：不许让阿禾知道。

头一天，十一月二十三日，星期一。健身房朝北，晚上七点，窗子外头黑透了，玻璃上映着一排器械和他自己。

他拿二十公斤的空杠热了身，加到四十，深蹲十个一组。头几组很顺，杠在肩膀上压着，往下蹲，往上站，镜子里那个人的腿看着也像一回事。蹲了十二组，一百二；再卧推三十公斤，六组——国庆那回在这张凳子上黑过一回，这回他没憋气，吸，绷住，推，吐，推得规规矩矩；引体向上拉了三个就挂住了，套上弹力带接着拉；坐姿推肩、哑铃弯举、臂屈伸，每样都练到抬不起来。组数他记在手机备忘录里，一行比一行长。十点关门，他是最后一个出去的，两条腿像两袋湿沙子，走下楼梯的时候，一级一级扶着栏杆。

心里却是满的。他想：这才叫练。半决赛那天，他要让她抬起头来看一眼——不是看一个凑数的。

第二天早上，闹钟一响，他想翻身，没翻动。两条大腿硬得像晾了一夜的油条，一弯就要断；上厕所蹲不下去，得扶着墙；胳膊举不过头顶，头洗了一半，泡沫在耳朵后头干了；胳膊肘伸不直，胸口后背一动就扯着疼。

中午下楼去食堂，六层没电梯，他是倒着下的：脸朝上，手扶栏杆，一级一级往后退，退得像一只怕摔的螃蟹。眼镜跟在后头看了半天：「忙哥，你这是在倒放？」

「我那是在倒行逆施。」沈芒说，「高手都这么下楼。」

傍晚院队训练，他照旧拄着拐坐在场边，单脚站，脚尖写字母。阿禾拿着本子从他跟前过，站住了：「你腿怎么了？脚踝不是这么走路的。」

「没怎么。」

「你上台阶，两条腿都在打弯。」

他脑子转得飞快：「护踝。勒的。」

阿禾低头看了看他的脚，看了半天，没说话，在本子上写了一行，走开了。沈芒出了一后背的汗。

他心里是有一本账的。她说别练，怕的是脚踝；他没跳，脚踝一下也没用上。她十月里教过他，肉是歇着长的，隔天练——这话他记得。可他算过了，隔天练，一个礼拜只练得了三回，来不及。再说，疼就是在长，这话他不知在哪儿看来的，这会儿想起来，觉得句句是真。他把这本账在心里翻来覆去地过了一遍，每一笔都站得住。

晚上他照去。深蹲还是四十公斤，十个一组，蹲到一百腿就打摆子；他咬着牙，一组一组数到三百，最后几组蹲得难看，腰先弓了；上身那几样又来了一遍，还加了一遍。备忘录里那一行，比头一天长出一截。

第三天早上六点，他躺着量晨脉，照规矩发给阿禾：八十八。平时七十上下。他看了一眼，倒还挺高兴：心跳得快，大概是气血旺。腿是软的，下楼歇了两回。

白天她没回。他想：没回，就是没事。

晚上七点四十，蹲到第二百个，手机一震：

「88？今天别练。」

他捏着手机，站在深蹲架底下，杠还在架子上。她说的是今天别练——她不知道他在练什么，她以为他在宿舍站单脚。要是现在停了，这三天就是两天半；两天半的闭关，小说里也没见过。他又想起她那本子上那一行，不知写的什么。他想了一会儿，回了一个字：

「好。」

那个字发出去，手机还没揣进兜，他心里就有一样东西沉了一下，像咽了一颗没剥壳的蛋。他没去看它。把杠扛上肩，蹲完了剩下的一百。备忘录里三天的组数，一天比一天长。

于是就有了那天夜里十一点的那一泡。

他在厕所里站了一分钟，到底没忍住，出来跟室友说：「我的尿，是可乐色的。」

老蔡从上铺探出半个脑袋：「你晚上喝可乐了？」

「喝了一罐。可这一泡的颜色，比我喝进去的那一罐还深。」

眼镜已经在搜了，脸色一点一点变了：「我查了。腿疼得碰不得、没劲、尿是可乐色——横纹肌溶解。没练过的肌肉猛加量，尤其是往下放、往下蹲那一段，肌纤维一根一根撕开——你这是全身好几块大肌肉一齐撕了——里头的肌红蛋白漏进血里；肾把它滤出来，尿就成了可乐色，滤多了，肾堵。马上去医院。」老蔡一脸肃穆：「走火入魔。」

眼镜一边穿鞋一边给阿禾打电话。沈芒扑过去夺手机，腿一软，没夺着。

十一点四十，校医院的值班大夫看了一眼他的尿杯，二话没说，叫了车，送城里的医院。眼镜陪他坐在后座；老蔡也跟来了，怀里抱着自己的枕头——他说万一要守夜。车顺着沂河往南开，岸上的灯一盏一盏往后退。沈芒靠在车窗上，腿疼得一跳一跳，心里想的却是另一件事：这下，她要知道了。

凌晨一点，急诊。胳膊上扎着针，头顶一袋盐水一滴一滴地落。大夫念化验单：「肌酸激酶，四万二。」沈芒问高吗。大夫说：「正常人一两百。」

走廊尽头的门开了。阿禾赶来了，一件长羽绒服，底下露着一截睡裤，球鞋没穿袜子，马尾扎歪了。她走到推床跟前，看了那袋盐水，看了那张单子，看了很久。然后她掏出本子，写了一行，合上。一个字也没说。

沈芒宁可她骂他。他小声说：「阿禾……」

她抬眼看他。他把后半句咽了回去。胸口那颗没剥壳的蛋，这会儿才真正硌到了他。

病床是四点钟才腾出来的。这中间，她一直坐在走廊的长椅上，羽绒服裹着，不说话，也不走。老蔡抱着枕头在她旁边睡着了，脑袋一点一点的。推床进电梯的时候，沈芒从门缝里看见她站起来，看着电梯门合上，才转身。她第二天早上有课。

大夫在旁边写病历，头也不抬：「住院，输液三天，多喝水。出院以后两个礼拜，不许剧烈运动。」

「半决赛是二十八号。」

「二十八号，你在这儿。」

住的是一间三人病房，十七床，靠门。

二十六日一早，眼镜来了，从兜里摸出那本卷了边的《抱朴子内篇》：「老蔡说你走火入魔。我回去翻了，葛洪那时候没有这个词，倒有一句比它准：『[力所不胜，而强举之，伤也]{典=baopu-jiyan-shang}。』」

「我举得动啊。三百个呢。」

眼镜拿指头点着那个「强」字：「你举得动的是那一下。这一篇数了十几样伤，末了一句是积伤至尽。伤不是哪一下伤的，是一天一天攒的。」

下午阿禾下了课来了。她在床尾坐下，从床头抽出一张输液单，翻到背面，先不说话，画了一条横线。

「这是你原来的样子。」她从横线往下画了一道弯，「练完了，你比练之前差：肉里有细伤，糖用光了，人是累的。练，是挖坑。」那道弯又慢慢爬上来，爬过横线，高出一小截，「歇好了，吃饱了，睡足了，身子把坑填平，还多填一截，防着下回再来——这一截，才是长出来的。」她在那一截顶上点了一个点，「下一回，在这儿练。一截一截，往上走。」

她又画了一条：往下弯，没等爬回横线，又往下弯；再往下，再往下，像三级往下走的台阶。

「你一个坑没填，又往下挖了两天。」她点着本子上那个八十八，「晨脉高一截，就是身子在跟你说：前一天的账还没还完。雷老师带了二十年队，就一句话：加量，一个礼拜最多加一成。你一天加一倍。」

沈芒看着那三级台阶，半天没出声。他忽然明白那个八十八是什么了。那天早上他看着它，还挺高兴，当是气血旺；原来它是身子在喊停。身子喊了，她也喊了——「今天别练」——两边都喊了，他回了一个「好」，扛起杠，又蹲了一百。

能不蹲的。他蹲了。

「这条线画得粗，」阿禾把输液单折好，夹进本子，「干我们这行的人还在争它准不准。拿来管你，够了。」

晚上老蔡和眼镜来了。眼镜拎着一摞纸，是这两天的课堂笔记，他拿正楷替他誊了一遍，连严老师的黑板都画了。老蔡抱着一只东西进门，病房里三张床一齐看过去：他奶奶寄的那只泡脚桶，带加热的。「我奶奶说，住院的人脚凉。」他把桶往床底下一塞，「护士不让插电。你拿凉水泡。」沈芒躺在床上笑，笑得胳膊上的针都晃了。院队群里，邢斌给他发了两个字：「好养。」大刘跟了一个大拇指——跟伤停名单底下那回一模一样。他把手机扣在胸口，扣了很久。

二十七号，什么事也没有。盐水一滴一滴地落，一袋换一袋。两条腿不敢碰，碰一下疼得龇牙；可他躺到下午，躺得浑身发痒。病房里能干的事，他数了一遍，只剩一样是阿禾许的。

他扶着输液架，站到床边的地上，把分量一点一点挪到右脚上，闭上眼。

头一回十几秒就晃了。他睁开眼，缓一缓，再闭。隔壁床的大叔放下手机看着他，看了半天，没敢问。第三回，他听见走廊里的推车声从左边过去，听见输液架上那袋盐水轻轻碰了一下杆子，听见自己的脚底板在往左歪、又自己扳回来——他没数，是护士进门看了一眼墙上的钟替他说的：「十七床，你这都站半分钟了，干吗呢？」

三十秒。阿禾说，站稳三十秒，才算接上。

他扶着输液架坐回床上，给阿禾发了一条：「单脚闭眼，三十秒。在病房。」

过了一会儿，回了一个字：「记。」

隔了一会儿，又来一条：「脚是接上了。腿还躺着。」

二十八号晚上，半决赛。他躺在病床上看手机直播，左手扎着针，右手举着手机，声音开到最小。针推对药学，第三节邢斌抽了筋，叫人架下去，替补一个一个都上过了——沈芒盯着手机，头一个念头是：要是我在，就该我上了。第二个念头跟着就来，比头一个还快：要是我在，我上得去么？第四节邢斌揉着小腿又上来了，一记中投拉开。针推赢了四分。他在床上「好」了一嗓子，护士从门口探进头来：「十七床！」他赶紧缩回被子里。镜头扫过替补席，十二只纸杯，他那只「0」也摆上了，扣着。

十二只。他不在，他们把他算上了。他躺在十七床上，胸口忽然涨得满满的，眼眶跟着就热了，赶紧拿手机挡住脸——隔壁床还看着呢。

另一场，中药学院赢了中医二十分，马小宝一个人拿了二十八分。散场以后，马小宝发来一张记分牌：「凑数的，决赛见。躺着可不算数。」

二十九日早上出院。结账的单子是他自己去交的：学生医保报了一大半，剩下的四百多块，把他十一月的生活费连底交了进去。家里，他一个字没提——爸的腿还在家里架着，这个月，家里不能再多出一笔。

阿禾在医院门口等着，手里拎着他那对拐——他住院那夜忘在六一七的，她从宿管阿姨那儿押了证取来的。她把拐递给他，又递给他一张纸，三条：晨脉回到七十以下，才许摸球；摸了球，只许罚球；十二月六号复查抽血。

「罚球也算练？」

「罚球不挖坑。」

两个人站在医院门口等车，等了好一会儿，谁也不说话。沈芒憋不住了：「阿禾，你还生气呢？」

阿禾看着马路对面：「你练，我不气。练坏了，我也不气，谁都有头一回。」她停了一下，「我气的是，那天我问了你，你说好。」

他张了张嘴，什么也没说出来。

「你的数，我天天记。」阿禾说，「数是你自己报的。你报了实话，又不听，那我这本子，记的是什么？」

车来了。她先上了车，没回头。沈芒跟在后头上了车，一路上把这几句话翻来覆去地过，比大夫那几句记得还牢。
story.en:
November 21st, Saturday, round three of the group stage. On the bench stood a row of paper cups, mouths down, numbers written on the bottoms — Ahe's rule: whoever had played came off for a drink and turned his own cup over. Shen Mang sat in the stands on his crutches and counted twice: eleven. His cup, "0", hadn't been set out.

Tuina won and topped Group A — into the top four; next year there would still be a Tuina team. Behind the scorer's table Ahe closed her notebook and pressed both hands flat on it for a long while before she opened it again. On the next court Chinese Pharmacy won too and topped Group B. When it broke up, Ma Xiaobao sauntered over and tapped his crutch with the shaker bottle: "Number Zero. A team registers twelve; one short and it can't enter — you're just here to make up the numbers." Neither of them mentioned that night in the rare-books room; if anything Ma Xiaobao was easier with him than before, as if to make up for it.

Not one word of it was wrong, which was why it hurt so much. His name had gone onto the Tuina roster at eleven forty on the night the list was due, when Ahe was one short and typed in his ID number. He gripped the crutch until his knuckles went white, and had to keep smiling; the rebound, that burning thing, met those two words like a splash of water, hissed, and went out.

But once the hurt passed, something in him quietly loosened: a number-filler, nobody watching, no need to step up to the free-throw line, no few hundred pairs of eyes fixed on him. The loosening startled him, and he hurried to push it back down, and told no one.

That night Old Cai's phone dangled down from the top bunk, its screen stopped on a line: "The youth went into seclusion for three days and came out two realms higher."

He stared at the line for a long time. He had no cave. Three days, he had.

The semifinal was on the 28th. Ahe had given him exactly one exercise: stand on one foot, eyes closed. In a week he had gone from three seconds to twenty-odd; Ahe said thirty was when the wires counted as reconnected. But what he needed her to see couldn't be only a foot that stood steady — a foot that stood steady was still a number-filler. He set himself a "three days of seclusion" too: up to the gym on the second floor at seven each evening, train till it closed at ten; nothing that jumped, for the ankle; everything else. The card from Mid-Autumn hadn't expired; at that hour the gym held only a few postgrad-exam students walking on the treadmills, and nobody knew him. One more rule: Ahe must not find out.

Day one, November 23rd, Monday. The gym faced north; at seven in the evening the windows were black, and the glass gave back a row of machines and himself.

He warmed up with the empty twenty-kilo bar, loaded it to forty, and squatted in sets of ten. The first sets went smoothly — the bar pressing on his shoulders, down, up — and the legs on the man in the mirror looked like they meant it. Twelve sets, a hundred and twenty; then bench press, thirty kilos, six sets — he had blacked out on this very bench over National Day, and this time he didn't hold his breath: in, brace, push, out, every rep by the book; pull-ups, three before he hung there, then a resistance band and more; seated press, dumbbell curls, dips, each until he couldn't lift his arms. He logged the sets in the notes app on his phone, each line longer than the last. At ten they closed, and he was the last out, legs like two bags of wet sand, taking the stairs down one step at a time with a hand on the rail.

Inside, though, he was full. This, he thought, is what training is. On the day of the semifinal she would lift her head and look — and not at a number-filler.

Next morning the alarm went and he tried to roll over and couldn't. Both thighs were stiff as fried dough sticks left out overnight, ready to snap at a bend; he couldn't squat on the toilet and had to brace against the wall; his arms wouldn't go above his head, so he washed half his hair and the foam dried behind his ears; his elbows wouldn't straighten, and chest and back pulled with every move.

Going down to the canteen at noon — six floors, no lift — he went backwards: face up, hands on the rail, retreating one step at a time like a crab afraid of falling. Glasses watched from behind for a good while: "Mang, are you on rewind?"

"This is called reversing the order of things," Shen Mang said. "Masters all take stairs this way."

At the department team's evening practice he sat at the side on his crutches as usual, standing on one foot, writing letters with his toe. Ahe came past with her notebook and stopped: "What's wrong with your legs? That isn't how you walk on a sprained ankle."

"Nothing."

"Both your legs bend when you take a step."

His mind raced: "The brace. It pinches."

Ahe looked down at his foot for a long moment, said nothing, wrote a line in her notebook, and walked on. Shen Mang's back was wet through.

He kept a ledger in his head. She had said don't train because she was afraid for the ankle; he hadn't jumped, hadn't used the ankle once. She had taught him in October that muscle grows while you rest — train every other day — and he remembered. But he had done the sums: every other day meant three sessions in a week, not enough. Besides, pain is growth — he had read it somewhere, and now that he recalled it every word rang true. He went through the ledger in his head again and again, and every entry held up.

That evening he went again. Still forty kilos on the squat, sets of ten; by a hundred his legs were shaking; he gritted his teeth and counted set by set to three hundred, the last few ugly, his back rounding first; then the upper body all over again, and once more on top. The line in his notes was a stretch longer than the day before.

Day three, six in the morning, he took his resting pulse lying down and sent it to Ahe as the rule required: eighty-eight. Normally around seventy. He looked at it and was rather pleased: a quick heart, probably the qi and blood thriving. His legs were soft; he rested twice on the way downstairs.

She didn't reply all day. No reply, he thought, means nothing's wrong.

At seven forty that evening, on the two hundredth squat, his phone buzzed:

"88? No training today."

He stood under the squat rack holding the phone, the bar still on the rack. She had said no training today — she didn't know what he was training; she thought he was standing on one foot in the dorm. If he stopped now, three days became two and a half, and two and a half days of seclusion wasn't in any novel. He thought of that line in her notebook, whatever it said. He thought for a moment and typed one character:

"OK."

The word went out, and before the phone was back in his pocket something inside him sank, like swallowing an egg with the shell still on. He didn't look at it. He shouldered the bar and finished the remaining hundred. Three days of sets in his notes, each day longer than the last.

Which is how there came to be that puddle at eleven that night.

He stood in the toilet a full minute, then couldn't hold it in and came out to tell his roommates: "My pee is the colour of cola."

Old Cai poked half his head out of the top bunk: "Did you drink cola tonight?"

"One can. But this is darker than the can was."

Glasses was already searching, and his face changed by degrees: "I looked it up. Legs too sore to touch, no strength, cola-coloured urine — rhabdomyolysis. Untrained muscle loaded hard all at once, especially on the way down, the lowering part — the muscle fibres tear one by one — and you've torn several big muscles all over your body at once — and the myoglobin inside leaks into the blood; the kidneys filter it out, which turns the urine cola-coloured, and filter too much and the kidneys clog. Hospital. Now." Old Cai, solemn: "Deviation. Fire and demons."

Glasses was dialling Ahe as he pulled his shoes on. Shen Mang lunged for the phone, his legs gave, and he missed.

At eleven forty the duty doctor at the school clinic took one look at his specimen cup and, without a word, called a car for the hospital in town. Glasses sat with him in the back; Old Cai came too, hugging his own pillow — in case, he said, there was a night watch. The car followed the Yi River south, the lights on the bank sliding back one by one. Shen Mang leaned on the window, his legs throbbing, and what he was thinking about was something else: now she'll know.

One in the morning, emergency. A needle in his arm, a bag of saline overhead dripping. The doctor read the lab sheet: "Creatine kinase, forty-two thousand." Shen Mang asked if that was high. The doctor said: "Normal is one or two hundred."

The door at the end of the corridor opened. Ahe had come — a long down coat with a strip of pyjama trouser showing underneath, trainers with no socks, her ponytail tied crooked. She walked up to the trolley, looked at the saline, looked at the lab sheet, looked for a long time. Then she took out her notebook, wrote one line, and closed it. She didn't say a word.

Shen Mang would rather she had shouted at him. He said quietly: "Ahe..."

She raised her eyes to him. He swallowed the rest. The egg with the shell on, in his chest, only now really dug in.

A ward bed didn't come free until four. All that time she sat on the bench in the corridor, wrapped in her down coat, not speaking and not leaving. Old Cai fell asleep beside her hugging his pillow, head nodding. As the trolley rolled into the lift Shen Mang saw through the closing gap that she had stood up, and watched the doors shut before she turned away. She had class the next morning.

The doctor was writing up the notes without looking up: "Admit him. Three days on a drip, plenty of water. No strenuous exercise for two weeks after discharge."

"The semifinal's on the 28th."

"On the 28th you're here."

A three-bed ward, bed seventeen, by the door.

Early on the 26th Glasses came, and from his pocket drew the dog-eared Inner Chapters of the Baopuzi: "Old Cai says you've suffered deviation — fire and demons. I went back and looked: Ge Hong didn't have that phrase in his day, but he had one that fits better: 'What the strength cannot bear, and yet one forces oneself to lift — that is injury.'"

"But I could lift it. Three hundred of them."

Glasses put his finger on the word "forces": "What you could lift was that one rep. This chapter lists a dozen kinds of injury, and the last line is: injuries accumulate until they are used up. An injury isn't one rep. It's a day at a time, adding up."

In the afternoon Ahe came after class. She sat at the foot of the bed, took an infusion slip from the headboard, turned it over, and without a word drew a horizontal line.

"This is how you were." From the line she drew a curve dipping down. "After training you're worse than before: fine tears in the muscle, the sugar used up, you're tired. Training is digging a hole." The curve climbed slowly back, crossed the line, and rose a little above it. "Rest well, eat enough, sleep enough, and the body fills the hole in — and fills a bit extra, against the next time. That extra bit is what you've grown." She put a dot at the top of it. "Next time, train from here. One bit at a time, upward."

Then she drew another line: down, and before it climbed back to the baseline, down again; then down, and down, like three steps descending.

"You hadn't filled one hole, and you dug for two more days." She tapped the eighty-eight in her notebook. "A resting pulse a notch high is your body telling you: yesterday's bill isn't paid. Coach Lei has run teams for twenty years and has one sentence: add load by a tenth a week at most. You doubled it in a day."

Shen Mang looked at the three descending steps and said nothing for a long time. Suddenly he understood what the eighty-eight had been. That morning he had looked at it and been rather pleased, taking it for thriving qi and blood; it had been his body calling a halt. His body had called it, and so had she — "no training today" — both of them had called it, and he had answered "OK", shouldered the bar, and squatted another hundred.

He could have not squatted. He squatted.

"This curve is drawn thick," Ahe said, folding the slip and tucking it into her notebook. "People in my field are still arguing over how exact it is. To keep you in line, it's enough."

That evening Old Cai and Glasses came. Glasses carried a sheaf of paper: two days of class notes, copied out for him in neat block script, Teacher Yan's blackboard drawn in as well. Old Cai came in hugging something, and all three beds turned to look: the heated foot-bath his grandmother had sent. "My grandma says people in hospital get cold feet." He shoved it under the bed. "The nurse won't let me plug it in. Use cold water." Shen Mang laughed in bed until the needle in his arm shook. In the team group Xing Bin sent him two characters: "Heal well." Big Liu followed with a thumbs-up — exactly as under the injury list. He laid the phone face-down on his chest and left it there a long time.

The 27th: nothing happened. Saline dripped, bag after bag. He didn't dare touch his legs — a touch made him bare his teeth — but by afternoon lying there made his whole body itch. He counted the things one could do in a ward, and only one was on Ahe's permitted list.

Holding the drip stand, he stood on the floor by the bed, shifted his weight bit by bit onto the right foot, and shut his eyes.

The first try wobbled in a dozen seconds. He opened his eyes, rested, shut them again. The man in the next bed put down his phone and watched him for a long while, not daring to ask. On the third try he heard a trolley pass left to right in the corridor, heard the saline bag tap lightly against the pole, heard the sole of his foot drifting left and hauling itself back — he wasn't counting; it was the nurse who came in, glanced at the wall clock, and counted for him: "Seventeen, you've been standing there half a minute. What are you doing?"

Thirty seconds. Hold thirty seconds, Ahe had said, and the wires count as reconnected.

He sat back on the bed with a hand on the drip stand and sent Ahe a message: "One foot, eyes shut, thirty seconds. In the ward."

A while later, one word came back: "Noted."

Then, after a pause, another: "The foot is hooked up. The legs stay in bed."

The evening of the 28th, the semifinal. He watched the phone livestream from his bed, needle in his left hand, phone in his right, the sound turned down to nothing. Tuina against Pharmacy; in the third quarter Xing Bin cramped and had to be carried off, and the subs had all been used one by one — Shen Mang stared at the phone, and his first thought was: if I were there, it would be my turn. The second thought came right behind, faster than the first: if I were there, could I have gone on? In the fourth quarter Xing Bin came back rubbing his calf and pulled away with a mid-range jumper. Tuina won by four. He let out a "yes!" from the bed, and the nurse put her head round the door: "Seventeen!" He ducked back under the blanket. The camera swept the bench: twelve paper cups, his "0" set out among them, face down.

Twelve. He wasn't there, and they had counted him in. Lying in bed seventeen, his chest suddenly swelled full and his eyes went hot with it, and he hurried to hide his face behind the phone — the next bed was still watching.

On the other court Chinese Pharmacy beat Chinese Medicine by twenty, Ma Xiaobao scoring twenty-eight by himself. Afterwards Ma Xiaobao sent a photo of the scoreboard: "Number-filler. See you in the final. Lying down doesn't count."

He was discharged on the morning of the 29th. He paid the bill himself: student insurance covered most of it, and the four hundred-odd yuan left took his November allowance down to the last coin. He said nothing at home — Dad's leg was still propped up there; this month the family could not take one more bill.

Ahe was waiting at the hospital gate holding his crutches — the pair he had left in 617 the night he was admitted; she had left her card with the dorm auntie to fetch them. She handed him the crutches, then a sheet of paper with three lines: resting pulse back under seventy before you touch a ball; once you touch one, free throws only; blood test on December 6th.

"Free throws count as training?"

"Free throws don't dig holes."

They stood at the gate waiting for the bus a good while without a word. Shen Mang couldn't hold it: "Ahe, are you still angry?"

Ahe looked at the far side of the road. "You trained — I'm not angry. You broke yourself — I'm not angry about that either; everyone has a first time." She paused. "What I'm angry about is that I asked you that day, and you said OK."

He opened his mouth and nothing came out.

"I write down your numbers every day," Ahe said. "The numbers are the ones you report. If you report the truth and then don't listen to it, what is this notebook of mine recording?"

The bus came. She got on first and didn't look back. Shen Mang climbed on behind her and turned those few sentences over and over all the way back, more firmly fixed than anything the doctor had said.

exits.means: waits for the morning pulse to come down before touching the ball

refuse.zh: 晨脉还没回到七十以下。
refuse.en: The morning pulse isn't under seventy yet.

story.zh:
七十六，七十二。什么也不许干，只许吃、睡、上课、躺着，他头一回知道歇着也要咬牙。十二月二日早上六点，六一七还黑着，他两根指头搭在腕子上，对着手机上的秒表数了两遍：六十九。他一骨碌坐起来，脑袋「咚」地撞在上铺床板上，捂着脑袋咧着嘴说：「出关了。」

上铺的老蔡被撞醒了，迷迷糊糊地问：「……几点了？」

他把六十九发给阿禾。阿禾回了一个字：「记。」

十二月七日下午，露天球场，北风刮得篮网横着飘。他摘了手套，十个指头冻得像十根胡萝卜，十投二。场边阿禾把本子合上：「歇了两礼拜，手生了。手生得快，熟得也快。一天两百个，投完回去泡脚。」铁丝网外头，马小宝背着球包走过去，站住看了他三个：一个砸筐，一个偏了，一个连筐都没碰着。「零号，你这是罚球，还是许愿？」「许愿。」马小宝笑了一声，走出去十几步，又回头看了一眼，没说话。

夜里，学校表白墙出了一条决赛竞猜，两支队二十四个名字，各跟一个百分数。他划到最末一行：

「0号　沈芒（针推）　上场概率：1%」

底下点赞最多的评论：「那1%，是怕他哭。」

他盯着那个「1%」看了很久，倒觉得这个数挺好：一百回里有一回，就是说，还有一回。他把那一行截了图，设成了手机的锁屏。往后每天早上躺着量晨脉，一按亮屏幕，先看见它。
story.en:
Seventy-six, seventy-two. Nothing allowed but eating, sleeping, classes and lying down, and for the first time he learned that resting takes gritted teeth too. At six in the morning on December 2nd, with 617 still dark, he laid two fingers on his wrist against the stopwatch on his phone and counted twice: sixty-nine. He sat bolt upright, banged his head on the boards of the top bunk, and said through a grin, clutching his head: "Out of seclusion."

Old Cai, jolted awake above him, mumbled: "...What time is it?"

He sent the sixty-nine to Ahe. Ahe replied with one word: "Noted."

The afternoon of December 7th, the outdoor court, the north wind blowing the net sideways. He took off his gloves, ten fingers frozen like ten carrots, and went two for ten. At the side Ahe closed her notebook: "Two weeks off; the hands have gone rusty. They rust fast, they come back fast. Two hundred a day, then home and soak your feet." Outside the wire fence Ma Xiaobao walked past with his ball bag and stopped to watch three: one off the rim, one wide, one that never touched iron. "Number Zero, is that free-throw practice or making a wish?" "Making a wish." Ma Xiaobao laughed once, walked a dozen steps, looked back once more, and said nothing.

That night the school's confessions wall put up a poll for the final: twenty-four names from the two teams, each with a percentage. He scrolled to the last line:

"No. 0  Shen Mang (Tuina)  chance of playing: 1%"

The top-voted comment underneath: "That 1% is in case he cries."

He stared at the "1%" for a long time, and decided it was rather a good number: one time in a hundred — which is to say, there's still one. He took a screenshot of the line and set it as his lock screen. From then on, every morning when he lay down to take his pulse and tapped the screen awake, it was the first thing he saw.
